docs.title: Objects
docs.text:
Object-oriented programming (OOP) is a way of organising a program around objects. An object can represent one particular thing the program needs to keep track of.

Imagine a school library with a physical copy of The Hobbit.

The program uses an object to keep the details of that book together. For example:

  • Title
  • Author
  • On loan?

docs.title: Polymorphism
docs.text:
In the previous chapters, we learned how inheritance allows subclasses to reuse and extend the properties and methods of a superclass.

Sometimes, a subclass needs to perform an inherited method differently.

Polymorphism allows the same method call to produce different behaviour depending on the type of object receiving it.

This is achieved through method overriding, where a subclass defines its own version of a method inherited from its superclass.

docs.title: Why Is Polymorphism Useful?
docs.text:
Our library system contains two types of books:

  • Book represents an ordinary book.
  • AudioBook represents an audiobook.

Both types of books need to provide a description.

However, an audiobook should also include its duration.

Rather than creating separate method names for each type of book, we can give both classes a method called get_description().

Each class can then provide the appropriate description.

docs.title: Method Overriding
docs.text:
Method overriding occurs when a subclass defines a method with the same name as a method in its superclass.

When that method is called on a subclass object, Python uses the subclass version instead of the inherited version.

The following program demonstrates this using our existing classes.

class Book:
    def __init__(self, title, copy_number):
        self.title = title
        self.copy_number = copy_number
        self._on_loan = False

    def get_loan_status(self):
        return self._on_loan

    def set_loan_status(self, status):
        if type(status) is bool:
            self._on_loan = status

    def get_description(self):
        return self.title + " #" + str(self.copy_number)


class AudioBook(Book):
    def __init__(self, title, copy_number, duration):
        super().__init__(title, copy_number)
        self.duration = duration

    def get_description(self):
        return self.title + " #" + str(self.copy_number) + " - " + str(self.duration) + " minutes"

Notice that both classes define a method called get_description().

The Book version returns the title and copy number.

The AudioBook version returns the title, copy number and duration.

Because AudioBook defines its own version, it overrides the method inherited from Book.

docs.title: Calling the Overridden Method
docs.text:
We can now create an ordinary book and an audiobook.

Add the following code below the class definitions.

book = Book("The Hobbit", 101)
audiobook = AudioBook("The Hobbit", 102, 680)

print(book.get_description())
print(audiobook.get_description())

Output:

The Hobbit #101
The Hobbit #102 - 680 minutes

Both objects receive the same method call:

get_description()

However, the result depends on the class of the object.

When book.get_description() runs, Python uses the method defined in Book.

When audiobook.get_description() runs, Python uses the overridden method defined in AudioBook.

This is an example of polymorphism.

docs.title: Polymorphism in UML Class Diagrams
docs.text:
A UML class diagram can show that a subclass overrides an inherited method.

The overridden method appears in both the superclass and subclass because each class defines its own version.

Method overriding in Book and AudioBook The Book superclass and AudioBook subclass both define get_description. A hollow triangular arrow points from AudioBook towards Book. Book + title: String + copy_number: Integer - on_loan: Boolean + get_loan_status(): Boolean + set_loan_status(status: Boolean): void + get_description(): String AudioBook + duration: Integer + get_description(): String

The hollow triangular arrow points towards Book, identifying it as the superclass.

The method get_description() appears in both classes because AudioBook overrides the superclass version.

The other methods are inherited and do not need to be repeated in the subclass.

docs.title: Using Polymorphism in a Loop
docs.text:
Polymorphism becomes particularly useful when a program works with several objects.

We can store different types of book objects in the same list and call the same method on each one.

Add the following code below the class definitions.

books = [
    Book("The Hobbit", 101),
    AudioBook("The Hobbit", 102, 680),
    Book("1984", 103)
]

for item in books:
    print(item.get_description())

Output:

The Hobbit #101
The Hobbit #102 - 680 minutes
1984 #103

docs.title: How the Loop Works
docs.text:
1. The list contains objects created from Book and AudioBook.
  2. On each iteration, item refers to the next object in the list.
  3. The program calls item.get_description().
  4. Python selects the correct method based on the object's class.
  5. The description is displayed.

Notice that the loop does not need to check whether an object is a Book or an AudioBook.

The same method call works for both types of object.

This is the main benefit of polymorphism: one method call can work with different types of objects, while allowing each type to behave appropriately.

docs.title: Method Overriding and Polymorphism
docs.text:
Although the terms are closely related, they describe different things.

Term Meaning Method overriding A subclass defines its own version of an inherited method. Polymorphism The same method call produces different behaviour depending on the object receiving it.

In our example, AudioBook overrides get_description().

When the loop calls get_description() on different objects, polymorphism allows Python to use the appropriate version.

Key Points

  • Polymorphism allows the same method call to produce different behaviour depending on the object.
  • Method overriding occurs when a subclass defines its own version of an inherited method.
  • An overridden method has the same name as the superclass method.
  • Python selects the appropriate method based on the object receiving the call.
  • Polymorphism allows programs to work with different types of objects without checking their class each time.
  • In UML, an overridden method appears in both the superclass and subclass.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
A property stores one piece of information about an object.

Every property has a name and a value.

The name identifies the information being stored, while the value is the information the object currently holds.

docs.title: Object Diagrams
docs.text:
An object diagram is a visual way of showing an object and the information stored about it.

The library book from the previous chapter provides an example of how properties store information about an object.

Book Name: The Hobbit Copy number: 101 On loan: Yes

The diagram has two compartments. The top identifies the object being represented. The lower compartment shows its properties and their current values.

In this example:

  • title stores "The Hobbit", the name of the book.
  • copy_number stores 101, the number used to identify this physical copy.
  • The on_loan property stores a Boolean value. True means the book is currently borrowed, while False means it is available.

docs.title: Working with Multiple Objects
docs.text:
A library may have several copies of the same book. Although the books have the same title, each physical copy needs to be tracked separately.

For example, the library has two copies of The Hobbit. One has been borrowed, while the other is available.

The computer system represents each copy as a separate object.

docs.title: Comparing two objects
docs.text:
Both objects store the same three properties: title, copy_number and on_loan.

First copy

Book title = "The Hobbit" Copy Number = 101 On loan = True

Second copy

Book title = "The Hobbit" Copy Number = 102 On Loan = False

The two objects have the same property names, but their values are not necessarily the same.

  • Both objects have the title "The Hobbit".

  • Their copy numbers are different because they represent different physical books.

  • Their loan statuses are different because only the first book has been borrowed.

This allows the library to track each copy independently.

docs.title: Object States
docs.text:
Each object stores its own property values. Together, these values make up the object's state.

When somebody borrows Book: Copy Number 102, its On Loan property changes from False to True.

Only the loan status of Book: Copy Number 102 has changed. Its title and copy number remain the same.

Book: Copy Number 101 is unaffected because it is a separate object with its own properties.

Note

This is an important feature of Object-Oriented Programming: changing the state of one object does not automatically change the state of another object.

docs.title: Finding Individual Objects
docs.text:
When a program contains several objects, it needs a way to identify which object it is working with.

An object reference allows the program to refer to a particular object.

For example, we could use:

  • copy1 to refer to Book 101.

  • copy2 to refer to Book 102.

These are simply names used by the program to distinguish between the two objects.

Accessing Properties in Python Python uses dot notation to access an object's properties.

For example: 

print(copy1.on_loan)
print(copy2.on_loan)

The first line displays the loan status of Book 101. The second displays the loan status of Book 102.

The output is:

True
False

We can also change the value of a property:

copy2.on_loan = True

This changes the loan status of Book 102.

Book 101 remains unchanged because copy1 and copy2 refer to separate objects.

Warning

The objects must already exist for this code to work.

We will learn how to create them when we study classes and instantiation.

docs.title: Classes
docs.text:
In the previous chapters, we learned that objects represent individual things in a program and store information using properties.

A library might have hundreds of books. Each book needs to store the same kinds of information, such as its title, copy number and loan status. However, the values stored by each book may be different.

Object-Oriented Programming uses classes to define the structure shared by these objects.

A class is a blueprint that defines the properties and methods that its objects will have.

docs.title: Why Do We Need Classes?
docs.text:
Imagine a library with 500 books. Every book needs to store three properties:

  • title – the name of the book.
  • copy_number – the number identifying a particular copy.
  • on_loan – whether the book is currently borrowed.

Rather than designing each book object separately, we can define a class called Book.

The class provides a common structure for every book object. Each object can then store its own values for the properties defined by that class.

This helps programmers keep their code organised and consistent.

docs.title: UML Class Diagrams
docs.text:
A UML class diagram is used to show the design of a class.

A class diagram is divided into three compartments:

  1. The top compartment contains the class name.
  2. The middle compartment contains the properties.
  3. The bottom compartment contains the methods.

The following diagram shows the design of the Book class.

Book + title: String + copy_number: Integer + on_loan: Boolean Methods introduced later UML class diagram showing the Book class and its properties.

docs.title: Understanding the Diagram
docs.text:
The class is named Book.

Its three properties are:

  • title, which stores a string.
  • copy_number, which stores an integer.
  • on_loan, which stores a Boolean.

The + symbol indicates that a property is public, meaning it can be accessed from outside the class.

Notice that the diagram shows property names and data types rather than actual values.

This is an important difference between an object diagram and a class diagram.

An object diagram shows the current values stored by one particular object.

A class diagram shows the structure shared by objects created from that class.

The bottom compartment is reserved for methods, which we will explore in a later chapter.

docs.title: Defining a Class in Python
docs.text:
Python uses the keyword class to define a class.

class Book:
    pass

Let's examine the code.

class is the Python keyword used to define a class.

Book is the name of the class. Class names normally begin with a capital letter.

: marks the beginning of the class body.

pass is a placeholder. It allows us to define the class without adding any instructions inside it yet.

At this stage, we have defined the Book class, but we have not created any book objects.

docs.title: Classes and Objects
docs.text:
It is important to understand the difference between a class and an object.

A class defines the structure that objects will share.

An object is an individual instance created from a class. Each object stores its own property values.

For example, the Book class can be used to create objects representing different copies of The Hobbit.

Although the objects share the same structure, each can have a different copy number and loan status.

Key Points

  • A class is a blueprint used to define objects.
  • A class defines the properties and methods its objects will have.
  • A UML class diagram shows the name, properties and methods of a class.
  • A class diagram describes structure, while an object diagram shows an object's current values.
  • Python uses the class keyword to define a class.
  • Defining a class does not automatically create an object.

docs.title: Instantiation
docs.text:
In the previous chapter, we learned that a class defines the structure shared by its objects.

However, defining a class does not automatically create any objects.

Instantiation is the process of creating an object from a class.

Each object created from a class is called an instance of that class.

docs.title: Creating an Object
docs.text:
The library uses a class called Book to represent its books.

We can create an object from this class by writing the class name followed by brackets.

book = Book("The Hobbit", 101)

The expression Book("The Hobbit", 101) creates a new book object.

The values "The Hobbit" and 101 provide the information needed to set up the object.

The variable book stores a reference to the newly created object. This allows the program to access the object later.

docs.title: Initialising an Object
docs.text:
When an object is created, its properties need starting values.

Python uses a special method called __init__ to initialise an object.

class Book:
    def __init__(self, title, copy_number):
        self.title = title
        self.copy_number = copy_number
        self.on_loan = False

The __init__ method runs automatically when a new Book object is created.

Let's examine its parts.

  • __init__ is the special method used to set the object's starting values.
  • self refers to the particular object being initialised.
  • title and copy_number are parameters that receive values when an object is created.
  • self.title = title stores the supplied title in the object's title property.
  • self.copy_number = copy_number stores the supplied copy number.
  • self.on_loan = False gives every new book a starting loan status of False.

Python automatically supplies self, so we only need to provide the title and copy number when creating a book.

docs.title: Creating Two Objects
docs.text:
We can use the same class to create more than one object.

book1 = Book("The Hobbit", 101)
book2 = Book("The Hobbit", 102)

Each call to Book() creates a separate object.

Both objects have the same properties, but they can store different values.

The diagram below shows the two objects after they have been created.

Book object 1 Book object 2 title = "The Hobbit" title = "The Hobbit" copy_number = 101 copy_number = 102 on_loan = False on_loan = False

The variables book1 and book2 refer to different objects.

Changing a property of one object does not automatically change the other.

docs.title: Accessing an Object's Properties
docs.text:
Once an object has been created, we can use its reference to access its properties.

book1.on_loan = True

print(book1.on_loan)
print(book2.on_loan)

The output is:

True
False

Only book1 has been changed.

Although both objects were created from the same class, they each store their own property values.

Key Points

  • Instantiation means creating an object from a class.
  • An instance is an individual object created from a class.
  • Python creates an object when the class is called, such as Book("The Hobbit", 101).
  • The __init__ method sets the object's starting values.
  • self refers to the object being initialised.
  • A variable such as book1 holds a reference to an object.
  • Each new class call creates a separate object.

docs.title: Methods
docs.text:
Previously, we learned how to define a class and create objects with their own properties.

Properties store information about an object. However, objects also need to carry out actions.

A method is a function defined inside a class. Methods define actions that objects can perform, such as returning information or changing property values.

docs.title: Defining a Method
docs.text:
Our library system needs to produce a label showing a book's title and copy number.

We can add a method called label() to the Book class.

class Book:
    def __init__(self, title, copy_number):
        self.title = title
        self.copy_number = copy_number
        self.on_loan = False

    def label(self):
        return self.title + " #" + str(self.copy_number)

The label() method is defined inside the Book class using the def keyword.

Notice that the method includes self as a parameter. This allows it to access the properties of the particular object using the method.

Inside the method:

  • self.title accesses the book's title.
  • self.copy_number accesses its copy number.
  • str() converts the copy number into a string so it can be joined with the title.
  • return sends the completed label back to the code that called the method.

The method does not change any properties. It uses the existing values to produce a result.

docs.title: Calling a Method
docs.text:
Once an object has been created, we can call one of its methods using dot notation.

Add the following code below the class definition:

book = Book("The Hobbit", 101)

print(book.label())

Output:

The Hobbit #101

The expression book.label() tells Python to run the label() method belonging to the object referenced by book.

Python automatically passes that object as self, allowing the method to access its properties.

The method returns the string "The Hobbit #101", which print() displays on the screen.

Notice the difference between accessing a property and calling a method:

  • book.title accesses a property.
  • book.label() calls a method.

The brackets () indicate that the method is being called.

docs.title: Methods That Change Properties
docs.text:
Methods can also change the values stored in an object's properties.

For example, when somebody borrows a book, the library system needs to update its loan status.

We can add a method called borrow() to the Book class.

def borrow(self):
    self.on_loan = True

This method changes the on_loan property of the object to True.

Unlike label(), the borrow() method does not return a result. Its purpose is to change the object's state.

To use it, we call the method on a book object:

book.borrow()

print(book.on_loan)

Output:

True

The method changes the loan status of the object referenced by book.

Other book objects are unaffected because each object stores its own property values.

docs.title: Methods in UML Class Diagrams
docs.text:
A UML class diagram shows the properties and methods defined by a class.

The diagram has three compartments:

  1. The class name.
  2. The properties.
  3. The methods.
Book + title: String + copy_number: Integer + on_loan: Boolean + label(): String + borrow(): void UML class diagram showing the properties and methods of the Book class.

The bottom compartment shows the methods available to objects created from the class.

The + symbol indicates that the methods are public.

The brackets identify each method and can contain any parameters it requires.

The return type appears after the colon:

  • label(): String means the method returns a string.
  • borrow(): void means the method does not return a value.

In Python, a method without a return statement returns None automatically.

docs.title: Putting It All Together
docs.text:
The following program combines both methods in the Book class.

class Book:
    def __init__(self, title, copy_number):
        self.title = title
        self.copy_number = copy_number
        self.on_loan = False

    def label(self):
        return self.title + " #" + str(self.copy_number)

    def borrow(self):
        self.on_loan = True


book = Book("The Hobbit", 101)

print(book.label())
print(book.on_loan)

book.borrow()

print(book.on_loan)

Output:

The Hobbit #101
False
True

The program creates a book object and displays its label and initial loan status.

It then calls borrow(), which changes the book's loan status to True.

The final print() confirms that the property's value has changed.

Key Points

  • A method is a function defined inside a class.
  • Methods describe actions that objects can perform.
  • Methods can access properties, change values or return results.
  • The self parameter refers to the object using the method.
  • Dot notation and brackets are used to call methods, such as book.borrow().
  • Methods appear in the bottom compartment of a UML class diagram.

docs.title: Encapsulation
docs.text:
In the previous chapters, we learned that classes group properties and methods together. Properties store information about an object, while methods allow the object to carry out actions.

Encapsulation is an Object-Oriented Programming principle that groups related properties and methods inside a class and allows access to the data to be controlled.

docs.title: Why Is Encapsulation Important?
docs.text:
Our library system uses a Book class to store information about each book.

Until now, we have changed the loan status directly:

book.on_loan = True

Although this works, it allows other parts of the program to change the value without going through the class's methods.

Encapsulation allows us to control how a property's value is accessed and changed.

For example, we can use methods to retrieve a book's loan status or update it when somebody borrows the book.

docs.title: Public and Private Members
docs.text:
A public member can be accessed from outside the class.

A private member is intended to be accessed only from within the class.

UML class diagrams use symbols to show visibility:

  • + indicates a public member.
  • - indicates a private member.

The following diagram shows a Book class with a private loan status and public methods.

Book + title: String + copy_number: Integer - on_loan: Boolean + get_loan_status(): Boolean + set_loan_status(status: Boolean): void The Book class uses public methods to provide controlled access to its private loan status.

The on_loan property is marked as private in the UML diagram.

The getter and setter methods are public, allowing other parts of the program to access or update the loan status through the class.

docs.title: Encapsulation in Python
docs.text:
Python commonly uses a leading underscore to indicate that an attribute is intended for internal use.

For example, _on_loan indicates that the loan status should normally be accessed through the class's methods rather than changed directly.

class Book:
    def __init__(self, title, copy_number):
        self.title = title
        self.copy_number = copy_number
        self._on_loan = False

The underscore is a naming convention. It does not prevent other code from accessing the attribute, but it tells programmers that the attribute is intended for internal use.

docs.title: Getter Methods
docs.text:
A getter method, also called an accessor, returns the value of a property.

We can add the following method inside the Book class:

def get_loan_status(self):
    return self._on_loan

The method returns the current loan status without changing it.

We can call it using:

print(book.get_loan_status())

If the book is available, the output is:

False

The program retrieves the value through the public method rather than accessing _on_loan directly.

docs.title: Setter Methods
docs.text:
A setter method, also called a mutator, changes the value of a property.

We can add the following method inside the Book class:

def set_loan_status(self, status):
    if type(status) is bool:
        self._on_loan = status

The method receives a new value through the status parameter.

Before updating _on_loan, it checks that the supplied value is a Boolean.

This is an example of validation. It prevents an unsuitable value from being stored.

To change the loan status, we call:

book.set_loan_status(True)

If the value passes validation, the setter updates _on_loan to True.

If the value is not a Boolean, the property remains unchanged.

docs.title: Putting It All Together
docs.text:
The following program demonstrates encapsulation using a getter and setter.

class Book:
    def __init__(self, title, copy_number):
        self.title = title
        self.copy_number = copy_number
        self._on_loan = False

    def get_loan_status(self):
        return self._on_loan

    def set_loan_status(self, status):
        if type(status) is bool:
            self._on_loan = status


book = Book("The Hobbit", 101)

print(book.get_loan_status())

book.set_loan_status(True)

print(book.get_loan_status())

Output:

False
True

When the object is created, _on_loan is set to False.

The getter returns the initial loan status.

The setter then checks the new value and changes the loan status to True.

The final getter call confirms that the property has been updated.

Key Points

  • Encapsulation groups related properties and methods inside a class and controls access to its data.
  • Public members can be accessed from outside the class and are marked with + in UML diagrams.
  • Private members are intended for internal access and are marked with - in UML diagrams.
  • Python uses a leading underscore as a convention for internal attributes.
  • A getter (accessor) retrieves a property's value.
  • A setter (mutator) changes a property's value.
  • Setters can include validation to prevent unsuitable values from being stored.

docs.title: Inheritance
docs.text:
In the previous chapters, we learned how classes define properties and methods, and how encapsulation can control access to an object's data.

Sometimes, different types of objects need many of the same properties and methods.

Inheritance allows a class to reuse the properties and methods defined in another class.

This reduces repeated code and makes programs easier to maintain.

docs.title: Why Is Inheritance Useful?
docs.text:
Our library system uses a Book class to represent books.

The library also lends audiobooks. An audiobook needs much of the same information as an ordinary book, including its title, copy number and loan status.

However, an audiobook also needs to store its duration.

Rather than repeating the shared properties and methods in a separate class, we can use inheritance.

The Book class is the superclass (parent class).

The AudioBook class is the subclass (child class).

The subclass inherits properties and methods from its superclass.

docs.title: Inheritance in UML Class Diagrams
docs.text:
A UML class diagram shows inheritance using a solid line with a hollow triangular arrowhead pointing towards the superclass.

The following diagram shows the relationship between Book and AudioBook.

Inheritance between Book and AudioBook Book is the superclass, shown above AudioBook. A solid line with a hollow triangular arrowhead points from AudioBook towards Book. Book + title: String + copy_number: Integer - on_loan: Boolean + get_loan_status(): Boolean + set_loan_status(status: Boolean): void AudioBook + duration: Integer AudioBook inherits from Book. The hollow triangle points towards the superclass.

The diagram shows two related classes.

Book is the superclass. It defines the properties and methods shared by books.

AudioBook is the subclass. It inherits from Book and can also have properties of its own, such as duration.

Notice that the shared properties and methods are not repeated in the AudioBook compartment. They are inherited from Book.

docs.title: Inheritance in Python
docs.text:
Python uses the superclass name in brackets when defining a subclass.

The following program defines a Book class and an AudioBook subclass.

class Book:
    def __init__(self, title, copy_number):
        self.title = title
        self.copy_number = copy_number
        self._on_loan = False

    def get_loan_status(self):
        return self._on_loan

    def set_loan_status(self, status):
        if type(status) is bool:
            self._on_loan = status


class AudioBook(Book):
    pass

The line:

class AudioBook(Book):

defines AudioBook as a subclass of Book.

The name Book in brackets tells Python which class to inherit from.

The pass statement means that we have not added any new code to the subclass yet.

Even though AudioBook does not define its own methods, it can use the methods inherited from Book.

docs.title: Using Inherited Properties and Methods
docs.text:
Add the following code below the class definitions.

audiobook = AudioBook("The Hobbit", 102)

print(audiobook.title)
print(audiobook.get_loan_status())

Output:

The Hobbit
False

The AudioBook class inherits the __init__() method from Book.

When the audiobook is created, the inherited initialiser sets its starting property values.

The get_loan_status() method is also inherited from Book.

This means we can call the method on an audiobook object even though it has not been defined again in AudioBook.

docs.title: Changing an Inherited Property
docs.text:
An audiobook can also use the inherited setter method to change its loan status.

audiobook.set_loan_status(True)

print(audiobook.get_loan_status())

Output:

True

The setter method changes the audiobook's loan status to True.

The getter method then returns the updated value.

Both methods are inherited from Book, so we do not need to write them again in AudioBook.

docs.title: Benefits of Inheritance
docs.text:
Inheritance offers several advantages.

  • Code reuse: Shared properties and methods can be defined once in the superclass.
  • Maintainability: Changes to inherited methods can also benefit subclasses.
  • Organisation: Related classes can be arranged into a clear hierarchy.

For example, if the library changes how loan status is managed, the shared methods can be updated in Book rather than separately in every subclass that inherits them.

Key Points

  • Inheritance allows a subclass to reuse properties and methods from a superclass.
  • A superclass is the class being inherited from.
  • A subclass is the class that inherits.
  • UML represents inheritance using a solid line with a hollow triangular arrowhead pointing towards the superclass.
  • Python uses the superclass name in brackets when defining a subclass.
  • A subclass can use inherited properties and methods without defining them again.
  • Inheritance reduces repeated code and improves maintainability.

docs.title: Subclasses
docs.text:
In the previous chapter, we learned that inheritance allows a subclass to reuse properties and methods from a superclass.

A subclass is a specialised class that inherits from another class. It can also define additional properties and methods of its own.

This allows programmers to reuse existing code while adding features needed by a particular type of object.

docs.title: Extending a Class
docs.text:
Our library system uses the Book class to represent books.

We have also introduced an AudioBook subclass, which inherits the properties and methods of Book.

An audiobook needs the same information as an ordinary book, including its title, copy number and loan status.

However, it also needs to store its duration.

We can extend AudioBook to include this additional property without repeating the code already defined in Book.

docs.title: Adding Properties to a Subclass
docs.text:
The following program builds on the Book class from the previous chapter.

class Book:
    def __init__(self, title, copy_number):
        self.title = title
        self.copy_number = copy_number
        self._on_loan = False

    def get_loan_status(self):
        return self._on_loan

    def set_loan_status(self, status):
        if type(status) is bool:
            self._on_loan = status


class AudioBook(Book):
    def __init__(self, title, copy_number, duration):
        super().__init__(title, copy_number)
        self.duration = duration

The AudioBook class now has its own __init__() method.

This allows it to receive an additional value for duration.

The line:

super().__init__(title, copy_number)

calls the superclass initialiser.

This sets up the properties inherited from Book, including title, copy_number and _on_loan.

The next line:

self.duration = duration

stores the additional property belonging to the audiobook.

The subclass does not need to repeat the instructions that initialise the shared properties.

docs.title: Creating an Audiobook Object
docs.text:
We can now create an audiobook with its own duration.

Add the following code below the class definitions.

audiobook = AudioBook("The Hobbit", 102, 680)

print(audiobook.title)
print(audiobook.duration)
print(audiobook.get_loan_status())

Output:

The Hobbit
680
False

The audiobook stores the title and copy number inherited from Book, along with its own duration property.

In this example, the duration is measured in minutes.

The get_loan_status() method is inherited from Book, so it can be called without being defined again in AudioBook.

docs.title: Understanding the Class Diagram
docs.text:
The following UML diagram shows how AudioBook extends Book.

Book and AudioBook class hierarchy Book is the superclass and AudioBook is the subclass. A solid line with a hollow triangular arrowhead points upwards and touches the Book class. Book + title: String + copy_number: Integer - on_loan: Boolean + get_loan_status(): Boolean + set_loan_status(status: Boolean): void AudioBook + duration: Integer AudioBook inherits the shared properties and methods of Book and adds its own duration property.

The hollow triangular arrow points towards Book, identifying it as the superclass.

The AudioBook compartment shows only the additional property, duration.

The inherited properties and methods are not repeated in the subclass diagram because they are already defined in Book.

docs.title: Adding Methods to a Subclass
docs.text:
A subclass can also define methods that are not available in its superclass.

For example, we could add a method to AudioBook that returns its duration.

def get_duration(self):
    return self.duration

This method belongs inside the AudioBook class and is not defined in Book.

It can be called using:

print(audiobook.get_duration())

Output:

680

To run this example, add get_duration() to the AudioBook class before creating the object.

This demonstrates that a subclass can inherit existing methods and introduce additional methods of its own.

Key Points

  • A subclass is a specialised class that inherits from a superclass.
  • A subclass can define additional properties and methods.
  • super().__init__() allows the subclass to use the superclass initialiser.
  • Inherited properties and methods do not need to be defined again.
  • A subclass can extend the functionality provided by its superclass.
  • UML inheritance arrows point towards the superclass.

docs.title: Parallel 1D Arrays
docs.text:
What You Need to Know

You must be able to describe, exemplify and implement parallel one-dimensional arrays.

docs.title: What Are Parallel Arrays?
docs.text:
Parallel arrays are two or more 1D arrays in which values at the same index are related.

Pupil Names and Marks
pupil_names = ["Peter", "Laura", "Marie"]
pupil_marks = [20, 21, 23]
Index pupil_names pupil_marks 0 Peter 20 1 Laura 21 2 Marie 23

Peter's name and mark are both at index 0. Marie's details are both at index 2.

Keep the Arrays in Step

The arrays must have the same length, and their values must remain in matching positions. If one array is reordered, the corresponding elements in every parallel array must also move.

docs.title: Accessing Related Values
docs.text:
Use the same index with each array:

Display One Pupil
index = 2

print("Name:", pupil_names[index])
print("Mark:", pupil_marks[index])

docs.title: Processing Parallel Arrays
docs.text:
An index-controlled loop allows the program to access matching elements:

Display All Pupils
for index in range(len(pupil_names)):
    print(pupil_names[index], pupil_marks[index])

Before processing, the program can check that the arrays have matching lengths:

if len(pupil_names) == len(pupil_marks):
    for index in range(len(pupil_names)):
        print(pupil_names[index], pupil_marks[index])
else:
    print("The parallel arrays do not match.")

docs.title: Reading Parallel Data from a CSV File
docs.text:
Suppose School-Reg.csv contains:

Peter,17,R1
Laura,16,R2
Marie,17,R1
Load Parallel Arrays
names = []
ages = []
registration_groups = []

with open("School-Reg.csv", "r") as file:
    for line in file:
        data = line.strip().split(",")

        names.append(data[0])
        ages.append(int(data[1]))
        registration_groups.append(data[2])

for index in range(len(names)):
    print(names[index], ages[index], registration_groups[index])

The age is converted to an integer as it is loaded. The with statement closes the file automatically.

docs.title: Choosing an Appropriate Structure
docs.text:
Parallel arrays are valid when a problem requires them, but they become difficult to manage as more related fields are added. A record keeps all the data for one entity together and is often a clearer solution.

Next: Records

docs.title: Records
docs.text:
What You Need to Know

You must be able to describe, exemplify and implement records.

docs.title: What Is a Record?
docs.text:
A record stores several related fields about one entity. Its fields can have different data types.

For example, one pupil record could contain:

Field Data type Example name String "Peter" age Integer 17 registration_group String "R1"

This differs from an array, whose elements normally represent values of the same type and purpose.

docs.title: Defining a Record in Python
docs.text:
Python does not have a separate record keyword. A dataclass provides a clear way to define a record-like structure.

Define a Pupil Record
from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass
class PupilRecord:
    name: str
    age: int
    registration_group: str

The definition specifies the name and data type of every field.

Records and Objects

Python implements this record using a class, but it is being used only to group data. Object-oriented classes containing constructors, private properties and methods are introduced later in the course.

docs.title: Creating a Record
docs.text:
Create One Record
pupil = PupilRecord("Peter", 17, "R1")

The values are supplied in the same order as the fields in the record definition.

docs.title: Accessing Fields
docs.text:
Use dot notation to access an individual field:

Access Record Fields
print(pupil.name)
print(pupil.age)
print(pupil.registration_group)

docs.title: Updating a Field
docs.text:
Update a Record
pupil.registration_group = "R2"
print(pupil.registration_group)

Only the selected field is changed.

docs.title: Complete Example
docs.text:
One Pupil Record
from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass
class PupilRecord:
    name: str
    age: int
    registration_group: str


pupil = PupilRecord("Peter", 17, "R1")
pupil.registration_group = "R2"

print("Name:", pupil.name)
print("Age:", pupil.age)
print("Registration group:", pupil.registration_group)

docs.title: Why Use a Record?
docs.text:
A record:

  • keeps related fields together
  • gives each field a meaningful name
  • supports different data types
  • is easier to maintain than several separate variables

One record stores one entity. To store several pupils, use an array of records.

Next: Arrays of Records

docs.title: Arrays of Records
docs.text:
What You Need to Know

You must be able to describe, exemplify and implement arrays of records.

docs.title: What Is an Array of Records?
docs.text:
An array of records is a one-dimensional array in which every element is a complete record.

Index 0 → one complete pupil record
Index 1 → one complete pupil record
Index 2 → one complete pupil record

Unlike parallel arrays, all fields belonging to one pupil remain together.

docs.title: Creating an Array of Records
docs.text:
Create Pupil Records
from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass
class PupilRecord:
    name: str
    age: int
    registration_group: str


pupils = [
    PupilRecord("Peter", 17, "R1"),
    PupilRecord("Laura", 16, "R2"),
    PupilRecord("Marie", 17, "R1")
]

The array has three elements. Each element contains the three fields defined by PupilRecord.

docs.title: Accessing and Updating Records
docs.text:
First use an array index to select the record, then use dot notation to select its field:

Access and Update Fields
print(pupils[1].name)  # Laura
print(pupils[1].age)   # 16

pupils[1].registration_group = "R3"

docs.title: Traversing an Array of Records
docs.text:
Display Every Record
for pupil in pupils:
    print(pupil.name, pupil.age, pupil.registration_group)

Only one loop is required because the array itself is one-dimensional.

docs.title: Inputting Records
docs.text:
Input Three Pupil Records
pupils = []

for count in range(3):
    name = input("Enter name: ")
    age = int(input("Enter age: "))
    registration_group = input("Enter registration group: ")

    new_pupil = PupilRecord(name, age, registration_group)
    pupils.append(new_pupil)

Each pass creates one complete record and appends it to the array.

docs.title: Records and Standard Algorithms
docs.text: Later in the course, the whole record can be moved during a sort or returned from a search. The algorithm compares one selected field, such as name or age, while keeping the complete record together.

docs.title: Parallel Arrays Compared with Arrays of Records
docs.text:
Parallel arrays Array of records Related data is split across several arrays Related data is kept in one record Matching indexes must remain synchronised The complete record moves as one element Becomes harder to manage as fields are added Easier to extend with additional fields

Next: Two-Dimensional Arrays

docs.title: Two-Dimensional Arrays
docs.text:
What You Need to Know

For Advanced Higher Computing Science, you should be able to:

  • describe and exemplify a two-dimensional array
  • declare and initialise a two-dimensional array
  • access and update an individual element
  • traverse rows and columns using nested loops
  • process data stored in a two-dimensional array
  • add rows and columns when using Python lists

docs.title: What Is a Two-Dimensional Array?
docs.text:
A two-dimensional array stores values in rows and columns. It can be pictured as a table, grid or spreadsheet. Every value is an element, located using a row index and a column index.

Python uses lists to represent arrays. A two-dimensional array is therefore a list containing other lists.

A 3 × 4 Seating Plan
classroom = [
    ["Alice", "Bob", "Charlie", "David"],
    ["Eve", "Frank", "Grace", "Hannah"],
    ["Ian", "Jack", "Katie", "Liam"]
]
Column 0 Column 1 Column 2 Column 3 Row 0 Alice Bob Charlie David Row 1 Eve Frank Grace Hannah Row 2 Ian Jack Katie Liam

Indexes Start at Zero

classroom[1][2] stores "Grace", because Grace is in row index 1 and column index 2.

docs.title: Why Use a Two-Dimensional Array?
docs.text:
Storing each row in a separate variable makes it harder to process the whole data set. A two-dimensional array keeps related values in one structure and allows one algorithm to process every row and column.

Typical uses include game boards, image pixels, seating plans, monthly figures for several branches and distances between locations.

docs.title: Key Vocabulary
docs.text: Term Meaning Element One value stored in the array Row A horizontal group of elements Column A vertical group of elements Index A number used to locate an element Nested loop A loop inside another loop Traverse Visit each required element in an array

docs.title: Continue This Topic
docs.text:
• Accessing and updating elements
  • Traversing and processing arrays
  • Adding rows and columns
  • Two-dimensional array tasks

Start with accessing and updating elements.

docs.title: One array, three separate objects
docs.text:
An array of objects is a collection in which each element holds a reference to an object. In Python, we use a list to implement it. A list can grow as the library adds more books.

Each position in the list has a number called an index. The diagram shows three positions in a list called books. The arrows show which object each position refers to.

books[0] ↓ refers to

Book Title: The Hobbit Copy number: 101

books[1] ↓ refers to

Book Title: 1984 Copy number: 102

books[2] ↓ refers to

Book Title: Coraline Copy number: 103

For example, the element at index 0 refers to The Hobbit, copy 101. The book's copy number identifies it in the library. The index tells the program where its reference sits in the list.

docs.title: Arrays of Records vs. Arrays of Objects
docs.text:
An array of records contains records, with each record storing a collection of related fields.

An array of objects contains references to objects created from a class. Each object has its own properties and can use the methods defined by its class.

For example, a Book object stores properties such as title, copy_number and _on_loan. It can also use methods such as get_description() and get_loan_status().

Array of Records Array of Objects Each element contains a record Each element refers to an object Records contain related fields Objects have related properties and methods Used to organise and process data Used to organise data and associated behaviour

The important difference is that objects combine data with the methods that operate on that data.

In the next lesson, you will learn how to create an array of Book objects in Python.

docs.title: Creating an Array of Objects
docs.text:
An array of objects allows a program to store and manage multiple objects using a single collection.

In our library system, each Book object represents a physical copy of a book, with its own title, copy number and loan status.

Python uses lists to store references to these objects. Objects can be created separately and then added to a list, or created directly inside the list.

This lesson explains how to create an array of Book objects and organise them using list indices.

docs.title: Step 1 – Define the Book Class
docs.text:
Before creating objects, we need to define the class they will be created from.

The following program uses the same Book class introduced in the Polymorphism chapter.

class Book:
    def __init__(self, title, copy_number):
        self.title = title
        self.copy_number = copy_number
        self._on_loan = False

    def get_loan_status(self):
        return self._on_loan

    def set_loan_status(self, status):
        if type(status) is bool:
            self._on_loan = status

    def get_description(self):
        return self.title + " #" + str(self.copy_number)

The class defines the properties and methods available to every Book object.

The __init__() method sets the initial property values when a new object is created.

The _on_loan property is initially set to False because a newly created book is not on loan.

We can now create objects from this class.

docs.title: Step 2 – Create Separate Objects
docs.text:
First, create three Book objects using separate variables.

Add the following code below the class definition.

book1 = Book("The Hobbit", 101)
book2 = Book("1984", 102)
book3 = Book("Coraline", 103)

Each call to Book(...) creates a separate object.

Variable Title Copy number book1 The Hobbit 101 book2 1984 102 book3 Coraline 103

Each variable refers to a different object.

Although all three objects are created from the same class, they have their own property values.

docs.title: Step 3 – Create the Array
docs.text:
We can now store references to these objects together in a Python list.

Add:

books = [book1, book2, book3]

The list is called books.

It contains three elements, each referring to one of the objects we created.

The objects are not copied when their references are placed in the list.

We can use len() to find the number of elements.

print(len(books))

Output:

3

The array contains three Book objects.

docs.title: Step 4 – Understand the Array Indices
docs.text:
Python list indices begin at 0.

Our array contains three positions.

Index Object reference Book 0 book1 The Hobbit 1 book2 1984 2 `book3

docs.title: Accessing and Updating Objects
docs.text:
An array index allows a program to select a particular object from a collection.

Once an object has been selected, dot notation can be used to access its properties or call its methods.

In our library system, this allows us to retrieve information about individual books and update their loan status.

docs.title: Accessing an Object
docs.text:
The books array contains three objects:

Index Title Copy number 0 The Hobbit 101 1 1984 102 2 Coraline 103

An index identifies the position of an object in the array.

For example:

books[0]

selects the first Book object.

Similarly:

books[2]

selects the third object.

Python starts counting array indices at 0, so an array containing three elements has valid indices of 0, 1 and 2.

docs.title: Reading an Object's Properties
docs.text:
We can combine an array index with dot notation to access a property belonging to the selected object.

Open your program from Creating an Array of Objects.

Keep the Book class and the array containing three books. Replace the final print() statement with:

print(books[0].title)
print(books[1].copy_number)

Output:

The Hobbit
102

The expression:

books[0].title

has three parts:

Part Purpose books Identifies the array [0] Selects the first object .title Accesses the object's title property

The same approach can be used to access other public properties.

For example:

print(books[2].title)
print(books[2].copy_number)

Output:

Coraline
103

Both instructions access properties belonging to the object at index 2.

docs.title: Calling an Object's Method
docs.text:
Objects also have methods defined by their class.

To call a method, we use dot notation followed by the method name and brackets.

For example:

print(books[2].get_description())

Output:

Coraline #103

The expression:

books[2].get_description()

first selects the object at index 2.

Python then calls its get_description() method.

The method uses the selected object's title and copy number to return a description.

Remember: Accessing a property retrieves a stored value. Calling a method executes instructions defined by the object's class.

docs.title: Updating an Object's Loan Status
docs.text:
The library needs to record when a book is borrowed.

Our Book class stores the loan status in the _on_loan property.

This property is managed using two methods:

  • get_loan_status() returns the current loan status.
  • set_loan_status() changes the loan status.

Suppose the book at index 1, 1984, is borrowed.

We can update its loan status using:

books[1].set_loan_status(True)

This selects the second object and calls its setter method.

We can check the result using:

print("Copy 102:", books[1].get_loan_status())

Output:

Copy 102: True

The loan status is now True, indicating that the book is on loan.

Using the setter method also reinforces encapsulation, because the class controls how its loan status is changed.

docs.title: Objects Maintain Their Own State
docs.text:
Each element in our array refers to a separate Book object.

Changing one object's loan status does not automatically change the others.

For example:

books[1].set_loan_status(True)

print("Copy 102:", books[1].get_loan_status())
print("Copy 101:", books[0].get_loan_status())

Output:

Copy 102: True
Copy 101: False

Copy 102 is on loan, but copy 101 remains available.

Both objects belong to the same class, but they maintain their own property values.

docs.title: Forgetting the Array Index
docs.text:
The array itself is not a Book object.

# Incorrect
print(books.title)

# Correct
print(books[0].title)

We must select an object before accessing its properties.

docs.title: Using an Invalid Index
docs.text:
Our array contains three objects.

# Incorrect
print(books[3].title)

This produces an IndexError because there is no element at index 3.

The highest valid index is 2.

docs.title: Forgetting the Method Brackets
docs.text:
# Incorrect
print(books[0].get_description)

# Correct
print(books[0].get_description())

The brackets are required to call the method.

Key Points

  • An array index selects an individual object.
  • Python list indices begin at 0.
  • Dot notation allows us to access an object's public properties.
  • Dot notation also allows us to call an object's methods.
  • Getter methods return information about an object's state.
  • Setter methods can update an object's state.
  • Each separately created object maintains its own property values.
  • Accessing an invalid index produces an IndexError.

docs.title: Processing Arrays of Objects
docs.text: Traversing a list means visiting its elements one at a time. A loop can display every entry in the catalogue or use each book's loan status to decide which entries to display.

docs.title: Visiting every book
docs.text:
Using the original three-book list, add this loop below your list and run it. On each iteration, book refers to the next object.

for book in books:
    print(book.get_description())

The Hobbit #101
1984 #102
Coraline #103

If you need each position as well as its object, loop over the indices. len(books) gives the number of entries and range(len(books)) gives the indices from zero up to the last valid position.

for index in range(len(books)):
    print(index, books[index].get_description())

0 The Hobbit #101
1 1984 #102
2 Coraline #103

docs.title: Adding a book and displaying loans
docs.text:
append() adds an entry at the end of a list. Pass it a new Book object to add a copy to the catalogue. The complete program below adds copy 104, displays the catalogue, then uses an if statement to display only the books on loan.

class Book:
    def __init__(self, title, copy_number):
        self.title = title
        self.copy_number = copy_number
        self._on_loan = False

    def get_loan_status(self):
        return self._on_loan

    def set_loan_status(self, status):
        if type(status) is bool:
            self._on_loan = status

    def get_description(self):
        return self.title + " #" + str(self.copy_number)


books = [
    Book("The Hobbit", 101),
    Book("1984", 102),
    Book("Coraline", 103)
]

books[1].set_loan_status(True)
books.append(Book("Noughts & Crosses", 104))

print("Catalogue")
for book in books:
    print(book.get_description())

print("On loan")
for book in books:
    if book.get_loan_status():
        print(book.get_description())

Catalogue
The Hobbit #101
1984 #102
Coraline #103
Noughts & Crosses #104
On loan
1984 #102

Create the list before the loops so both loops work with the same catalogue. In the second loop, the description is displayed only when the getter returns True.

Use a direct loop to visit the objects, or an index loop when you need their positions. Append new objects and use their current values to decide which entries to process.

docs.title: Arrays of Objects and Polymorphism
docs.text: An AudioBook is a subclass of Book. It has a duration and overrides get_description() to include that duration. Because both classes provide this method, a list can contain both kinds of object and a single loop can display their descriptions.

docs.title: One loop, two descriptions
docs.text:
Keep the Book definition from the previous lesson. Add the AudioBook definition below it and replace the code after the class definitions with this list and loop.

class AudioBook(Book):
    def __init__(self, title, copy_number, duration):
        super().__init__(title, copy_number)
        self.duration = duration

    def get_description(self):
        return self.title + " #" + str(self.copy_number) + " - " + str(self.duration) + " minutes"


books = [
    Book("The Hobbit", 101),
    AudioBook("The Hobbit", 102, 680),
    Book("Coraline", 103)
]

for book in books:
    print(book.get_description())

The Hobbit #101
The Hobbit #102 - 680 minutes
Coraline #103

The loop makes the same call for each item. Python uses Book.get_description() for copies 101 and 103 and the overridden AudioBook.get_description() for copy 102. This is polymorphism. The loop needs only the shared method name.

Each object supplies the version of the method appropriate to its class. The list and the loop work with both kinds of book.

docs.title: Bubble Sort
docs.text:
What You Need to Know

You must be able to describe, exemplify and implement bubble sort, and read and explain code that uses it.

docs.title: What Is Bubble Sort?
docs.text:
Bubble sort repeatedly compares neighbouring elements. If they are in the wrong order, it swaps them. After each pass, the largest unsorted value has moved to its correct position at the end of the array.

Bubble Sort a 1D Array
numbers = [7, 2, 5, 3, 4]

for pass_number in range(len(numbers) - 1):
    for index in range(len(numbers) - 1 - pass_number):
        if numbers[index] > numbers[index + 1]:
            temporary = numbers[index]
            numbers[index] = numbers[index + 1]
            numbers[index + 1] = temporary

print(numbers)

Output:

[2, 3, 4, 5, 7]

docs.title: How the Loops Work
docs.text:
• The outer loop controls the passes through the array.
  • The inner loop compares neighbouring elements.
  • pass_number shortens each pass because the values at the end are already sorted.
  • The entire array is sorted when all required passes are complete.

docs.title: Sorting Records
docs.text:
The same algorithm can compare a field in an array of records. When two fields are out of order, the complete records must be swapped.

Bubble Sort Records by Score
from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass
class PupilRecord:
    name: str
    score: int


pupils = [
    PupilRecord("Anna", 68),
    PupilRecord("Ben", 81),
    PupilRecord("Cara", 74)
]

for pass_number in range(len(pupils) - 1):
    for index in range(len(pupils) - 1 - pass_number):
        if pupils[index].score > pupils[index + 1].score:
            temporary = pupils[index]
            pupils[index] = pupils[index + 1]
            pupils[index + 1] = temporary

for pupil in pupils:
    print(pupil.name, pupil.score)

The algorithm compares the score field but swaps each complete record. The resulting array is ordered by score and is ready for a binary search using that same field.

docs.title: 1d Array Bubble Sort
docs.text:
A primary school is asking pupils to measure the outside temperature every day at noon. The temperatures will be recorded and sorted into ascending order.

The procedure will use a bubble sort algorithm to sort the following data, stored in an array. 

    [28.2, 24.8, 21.3, 25.0, 23.4, 27.1, 25.0]

(a) At the end of which pass of the algorithm would the state of the array be as shown below? [24.8, 21.3, 25.0, 23.4, 27.1, 25.0, 28.2]

(b) Create the program, showing the state of the array at the end of each pass.

docs.title: 1d Array Bubble Sort
docs.text:
Kofi has written a program to sort an array of data into descending order. The algorithm is a version of bubble sort and is shown in pseudocode below. 

# Initialise variables
items = [28, 40, 21, 25, 30, 27, 25]

num_items = len(items)
temp = 0
pass_number = 1
swapped = True

# Continue while swaps have been made and passes remain
while swapped and pass_number <= num_items - 1:
    swapped = False

    for index in range(num_items - 1):
        # Check whether adjacent items are out of order
        if items[index] > items[index + 1]:
            # Swap the items
            temp = items[index]
            items[index] = items[index + 1]
            items[index + 1] = temp

            swapped = True

    pass_number += 1

docs.title: Insertion Sort
docs.text:
What You Need to Know

You must be able to describe, exemplify and implement insertion sort, and read and explain code that uses it.

docs.title: What Is Insertion Sort?
docs.text:
Insertion sort builds a sorted section at the beginning of an array. Starting with the second element, it:

  1. stores the current value
  2. shifts larger values in the sorted section one position to the right
  3. inserts the stored value into the gap
  4. repeats for every remaining element

Shift, Then Insert

This implementation shifts elements to make a gap. It does not repeatedly swap neighbouring values like bubble sort.

docs.title: Sorting a 1D Array
docs.text:
Insertion Sort a 1D Array
scores = [7, 2, 5, 3, 4]

for index in range(1, len(scores)):
    current_score = scores[index]
    position = index - 1

    while position >= 0 and scores[position] > current_score:
        scores[position + 1] = scores[position]
        position -= 1

    scores[position + 1] = current_score

print(scores)

Output:

[2, 3, 4, 5, 7]

docs.title: How the Variables Work
docs.text: Variable Purpose index Selects the next element from the unsorted section current_score Temporarily stores the value being inserted position Moves backwards through the sorted section

docs.title: Sorting Parallel Arrays
docs.text:
When parallel arrays are sorted, every corresponding value must move with the sort key:

Sort Parallel Arrays by Score
names = ["Anna", "Ben", "Cara"]
scores = [85, 72, 90]

for index in range(1, len(scores)):
    current_score = scores[index]
    current_name = names[index]
    position = index - 1

    while position >= 0 and scores[position] > current_score:
        scores[position + 1] = scores[position]
        names[position + 1] = names[position]
        position -= 1

    scores[position + 1] = current_score
    names[position + 1] = current_name

for index in range(len(names)):
    print(names[index], scores[index])

docs.title: Sorting an Array of Records
docs.text:
An array of records is easier to manage because each complete record moves as one element:

Sort Records by Score
from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass
class PupilRecord:
    name: str
    score: int


pupils = [
    PupilRecord("Anna", 85),
    PupilRecord("Ben", 72),
    PupilRecord("Cara", 90)
]

for index in range(1, len(pupils)):
    current_pupil = pupils[index]
    position = index - 1

    while position >= 0 and pupils[position].score > current_pupil.score:
        pupils[position + 1] = pupils[position]
        position -= 1

    pupils[position + 1] = current_pupil

for pupil in pupils:
    print(pupil.name, pupil.score)

The score field is compared, but the complete PupilRecord is shifted and inserted.

docs.title: Bubble Sort Compared with Insertion Sort
docs.text:
Bubble sort Insertion sort Repeatedly compares neighbours Compares the current value with the sorted section Swaps values that are out of order Shifts values, then inserts the current value Largest unsorted value moves to the end after a pass Sorted section grows from the beginning

Both algorithms produce sorted data suitable for binary search.

docs.title: Binary Search
docs.text:
What You Need to Know

Describe, exemplify and implement:

  • Binary search

Read, trace and explain code that uses binary search.

docs.title: What is Binary Search?
docs.text:
Binary search is a searching algorithm that repeatedly divides a sorted list in half until the target value is found.

Unlike a linear search, binary search:

  • Requires the data to be sorted
  • Eliminates half of the remaining values after each comparison
  • Is significantly faster for large datasets

Important

Binary search only works correctly on sorted data.

docs.title: How Binary Search Works
docs.text:
Suppose we want to find the value 23.

[3] [7] [12] [18] [23] [29] [34] [41] [50]
                 ↑
               Middle
  1. Find the middle value.
  2. Compare the middle value with the target.
  3. If the target is smaller, search the left half.
  4. If the target is larger, search the right half.
  5. Repeat until the value is found.

docs.title: Worked Example
docs.text:
Suppose we want to find the value 34.

[3] [7] [12] [18] [23] [29] [34] [41] [50]

docs.title: Step 1
docs.text:
Middle value = 23

34 is greater than 23, so search the right half.

[29] [34] [41] [50]

docs.title: Step 2
docs.text:
Middle value = 34

Target found.

The search is complete.

docs.title: Why Was 34 Accepted if it Was Not the Middle Value?
docs.text:
A common misunderstanding is that binary search is looking for a value that is always in the middle of the original list.

This is not true.

Binary search repeatedly reduces the search area and then calculates a new middle position.

docs.title: Step 1
docs.text:
Index:  0  1   2   3   4   5   6   7   8
Value: [3][7][12][18][23][29][34][41][50]

The algorithm starts with:

low = 0
high = 8
mid = (low + high) // 2
mid = 4

The middle position is index 4, which contains the value 23.

Since 34 is greater than 23, everything to the left of 23 can be ignored.

docs.title: Step 2
docs.text:
The remaining search area is:

Index:  5   6   7   8
Value: [29][34][41][50]

Notice that there are now four values remaining.

With an even number of values there is no single middle value.

Binary search solves this problem using integer division (//), which always rounds down.

mid = (5 + 8) // 2
mid = 6

Index 6 contains the value 34.

The target has been found.

docs.title: Important
docs.text:
Binary search always calculates the middle index, not the middle value.

If there are two possible middle positions, integer division causes the algorithm to choose the lower index.

This guarantees that the search area becomes smaller every time the algorithm runs.

docs.title: Why Must Data Be Sorted?
docs.text:
Binary search works by eliminating half of the remaining data after each comparison.

This is only possible when the data is stored in order.

For example, if the middle value is 23 and the target value is 34, binary search knows that 34 must be to the right of 23.

Without sorted data, this assumption would be incorrect and the algorithm could miss the target value completely.

docs.title: Binary Search of Integers
Trace Table Example
docs.text:
Searching for the value 34:

Low High Mid Value at Mid Action 0 8 4 23 Search right half 5 8 6 34 Found

Trace tables are commonly used to explain how binary search works step by step.

Explanation low and high Store the current search boundaries. mid Stores the middle position. Target Found Return the index immediately. Target Smaller Search the left half of the list. Target Larger Search the right half of the list.

docs.title: Binary Search of Strings
Binary Search of an Array of Records
docs.text:
An array of records is still a one-dimensional sequence. The records must be sorted by the same field that the binary search compares.

Search Records by Name
from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass
class Pupil:
    name: str
    score: int


# The records are already sorted by name.
pupils = [
    Pupil("Anna", 68),
    Pupil("Ben", 81),
    Pupil("Cara", 74),
    Pupil("David", 59),
    Pupil("Eilidh", 77)
]


def binary_search_by_name(pupils, target):
    low = 0
    high = len(pupils) - 1

    while low <= high:
        middle = (low + high) // 2

        if pupils[middle].name == target:
            return middle
        elif target < pupils[middle].name:
            high = middle - 1
        else:
            low = middle + 1

    return -1


position = binary_search_by_name(pupils, "Cara")

if position != -1:
    print(pupils[position])
else:
    print("Pupil not found")

The algorithm compares the name field but returns the position of the complete record. If the program searched by score instead, the records would first need to be sorted by score.

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
• Faster than linear search for large datasets
  • Reduces the number of comparisons required
  • Efficient when data is already sorted

docs.title: Disadvantages
docs.text:
• Requires data to be sorted first
  • More complex to implement than linear search
  • Less efficient for very small datasets

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Feature Binary Search Data Sorted Required Method Repeatedly divides data in half Speed Fast for large datasets Complexity More complex than linear search

Binary search completes the algorithm sequence. Bubble sort or insertion sort can prepare unsorted data, provided the sort and search use the same value or record field.

CPU ALU Pixel NOT gate Binary LAN Register Cache Protocol

A developer wants to simulate a simple version of Battleships.

  • one cruiser that has size two
  • one destroyer that has size one

A player makes a guess to see if a ship, or part of a ship, is located at a particular location. If a ship is found at the location, then the player has hit the ship at this location.

docs.title: Brief
docs.text:
A black and white image can be represented as a two-dimensional array where:

  • 0 represents a white pixel
  • 1 represents a black pixel

Two images are exact inverses of each other if:

  • every white pixel in the first image is black in the second image
  • every black pixel in the first image is white in the second image

A developer has started to create an algorithm that compares two 3 x 3 black and white images, image1 and image2, to see if they are exact inverses of each other.

Complete the algorithm so that, when it ends, the value of the variable inverse is True if the two images are inverses of each other, or False if they are not.

The algorithm should work for any 3 x 3 black and white images stored in image1 and image2.

Indexing starts at zero.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
Your solution should:

  • compare every position in the two 3 x 3 arrays
  • check that each pair of pixels is opposite
  • set inverse to False if any pair is not opposite
  • leave inverse as True only when every pair matches the inverse rule
